title: Man charged with arson after cars torched outside Liberal MP's home: police
sourceDescription: Toronto police say they have arrested and charged a man in connection to an arson investigation after several cars were torched at the home of a Scarborough MP last week.
sourceBodyText:

Roshvin Crofton, 24, is charged in connection with an alleged arson that happened outside a Liberal MP's home in Scarborough last week. (Toronto Police Service) Social Sharing A man has been charged after several cars were torched at the home of a Scarborough MP last week, Toronto police say.

Roshvin Crofton, 24, was arrested Sunday. He is charged with arson causing damage to property, mischief over $5,000, conspiracy to commit an indictable offence, possession of incendiary material, and failure to comply with probation order, police said in a news release Friday.

A 2025 Hyundai Sonata, believed to be involved in the incident, was also seized. Police are looking for information on where the vehicle was in the days before the alleged arson.

Police say they are searching for a second suspect as well.

The alleged arson occurred in the driveway of Liberal MP Salma Zahid's home. Zahid represents the federal riding of Scarborough Centre-Don Valley East.

August 27 | Duration 2:02 Toronto police are investigating a suspected arson at the home of a Liberal Member of Parliament. Multiple cars on Salma Zahid's driveway were set on fire overnight. The Scarborough MP says the incident has left her shaken and worried about the safety of her family and staff. CBC’s Greg Ross takes us through what happened. Police say an "unknown suspect" approached the vehicles in the driveway early on Aug. 27, poured an accelerant on them and ignited two vehicles, causing them to catch fire, before fleeing the scene.

A third vehicle was damaged from the flames, police said.

Zahid thanked Toronto police in a statement released Friday, shortly after they announced the arrest.

"I welcome word of an arrest and charges related to the arson incident outside my home on August 27th, and news the police are seeking an additional suspect in relation to this case," she said.

"As the investigation is ongoing, we still do not have information with regards to a motive for this incident."

Toronto police seized a car believed to be involved in the incident. They are looking for information about its whereabouts in the days leading up to Crofton's arrest. (Toronto Police Service) Zahid, a Liberal backbencher, has been an MP for Scarborough Centre since 2015. She currently chairs the standing committee on science and research and is the vice-chair of the Canada-China legislative association.

The incident drew condemnation from numerous politicians, including Prime Minister Mark Carney.

title: PQ Leader accuses Ottawa of election interference to help Coalition Avenir Québec
sourceDescription: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon pointed to announcements Carney has made alongside Premier Christine Fréchette ahead of Oct. 5 vote
sourceBodyText:
Find clarity in the chaos. Subscribe now and save 70% SUBSCRIBE FROM $0.99/WEEK Digital access Digital + home delivery Parti Québécois Leader accuses Ottawa of election interference to help Coalition Avenir Québec Maura Forrest and Eric Andrew-Gee Published Yesterday Updated 2 hours ago Open this photo in gallery: Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, shown in the town of Lanoraie on Tuesday, said the federal Liberals largely ignored the requests of the Quebec government until the eve of the provincial election, set for Oct. 5. Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press

The leader of the sovereigntist Parti Québécois has accused the federal government of interfering in the Quebec election campaign to benefit the governing Coalition Avenir Québec, which is making a surprise comeback amid fears about the Canada-U.S. trade war.

Paul St-Pierre Plamondon suggested Friday that it’s no coincidence Prime Minister Mark Carney has made several recent announcements alongside Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette, ahead of a campaign in which the PQ is promising a third referendum on independence.

He said the federal Liberals largely ignored the requests of the CAQ government until the eve of the provincial election, which is scheduled for Oct. 5.

“I think we should be concerned about the possibility that this could be the greatest federal interference in our affairs and our election since 1995,” he told reporters in response to questions at a press conference in the northern town of Chibougamau. Quebeckers narrowly voted to remain in Canada during the 1995 referendum, and sovereigntists have long accused Ottawa of improperly meddling in the campaign.

Ms. Fréchette appears to have resuscitated her party as the trade dispute with the United States casts a long shadow over the campaign, and the CAQ now presents a real threat to the PQ.

U.S. businesses think looming countertariffs will inflict pain, but not misery

Before she was elected leader in April, the CAQ had collapsed in the polls and was projected to lose most or all of its seats in the upcoming election. But she has since positioned herself as a steady hand at the wheel in a time of crisis, and as someone who can work with Ottawa. Her leadership has drawn comparisons to Mr. Carney’s revival of the federal Liberals last year.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, meanwhile, has worked to shift the focus of the campaign off his promise to hold another sovereignty referendum in a first mandate. His party has led in the polls for the better part of three years, but support for independence in Quebec is low, hovering around 30 per cent.

In August, he promised not to hold a vote on separation while U.S. President Donald Trump is in office.

Accompanied by Ms. Frechette, Mr. Carney announces a $11-billion contract for icebreakers at the Davie shipyard in Levis, Que., on Aug. 24. Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press

Mr. Carney has appeared alongside Ms. Fréchette several times recently. Last month, they both travelled to St. John’s to unveil a new energy deal between Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador. Soon after, Mr. Carney announced an $11-billion contract with Quebec’s Davie shipyard to build icebreakers.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon said the “love-in” for Quebec marks a change from Ottawa’s previously dismissive attitude to the CAQ government, in power since 2018. He said Quebeckers should not “turn a blind eye” to the federal government’s “sudden interest in issues that had been stalled for eight years.”

Ms. Fréchette rejected the PQ Leader’s claims, saying there is “absolutely no” federal interference in the Quebec election. “The Parti Québécois seems to see a conspiracy where none exists. I’ve secured benefits from Ottawa through partnerships,” she told reporters. “What the Parti Québécois is really looking for is a fight.”

A spokesperson from the Prime Minister’s Office, in a statement, denied any election interference and said the government works with all premiers.

“The federal government does not interfere in provincial elections, and we will work with the Government of Québec to achieve these goals, regardless of which party is elected on October 5 th ,” read the statement.

This is not the first time Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has accused the Prime Minister of taking an interest in Quebec for political ends. When Mr. Carney visited the province in June to announce infrastructure funding deals worth nearly $10-billion, the PQ Leader said he was trying to undermine support for sovereignty.

More recently, he cast doubt on Mr. Carney’s claim that French-language protections were one of the reasons trade talks broke down with the U.S., saying the Prime Minister was trying to present himself as the defender of the French language.

More than 300 Via Rail cars will be built in Canada in shift to domestic production, Carney says

Last week, U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Mr. Carney manufactured the language dispute to keep the PQ from winning the Quebec election.

Mr. Carney remains very popular in Quebec. Earlier this week, the Liberals easily won a by-election in the province’s Saguenay region, taking more than 50 per cent of the vote in what was expected to be a tight race with the Bloc Québécois.

Jack Jedwab, president of the Montreal-based Association for Canadian Studies, a non-profit think tank, said any comparison with federal involvement in the 1995 referendum is “laughable.” The federal government has had a low profile in the election campaign, he added.

Mr. Jedwab said Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon is trying to “lean into the friction with the federal government” as a tactic to gain momentum and defend his narrow polling lead.

title: PM says 'more can be done' to address increasingly severe wildfire seasons
sourceDescription: Prime Minister Mark Carney says “more can be done” to address increasingly severe wildfire seasons in northwestern Ontario. This year is already being described as Ontario’s worst wildfire season on record, with the greatest impact occuring in the northwest of the province.
sourceBodyText:
Listen to this article Estimated 4 minutes The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. PM Mark Carney speaks on northwestern Ontario wildfire season

September 4 | Duration 2:01 Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Thursday and was asked about the federal government’s strategy to protect communities from wildfires, after two First Nations in the region were destroyed earlier this summer. Here’s his response. Social Sharing Prime Minister Mark Carney has promised new investments in early warning and detection of wildfires as Ontario faces its worst ever year for fires.

CBC News asked Carney about his approach to wildfires while he was in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Thursday to announce a major investment in Via Rail.

“What more can be done? We have made major investments and we have more to come in terms of early warning and detection,” Carney said.

This year is already being described as Ontario’s worst wildfire season on record, with the northwest of the province the worst affected area. More than 2,800 people from the region were displaced at the peak of this year’s wildfire activity, affecting well over a dozen communities.

Wildfires destroyed two First Nation communities in northwest Ontario this summer: Namaygoosisagagun First Nation (also known as Collins First Nation) and Whitewater Lake First Nation.

Ontario wildland firefighters greet Prime Minister Mark Carney at the Thunder Bay Fire Management Centre in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Thursday. (David Jackson/The Canadian Press) “I think we have to recognize, certainly do recognize this is the worst forest fire season in Ontario history — but the dynamics unfortunately are such that that record may be broken, and we're preparing for that possibility,” Carney said.

Carney thanked those on the front lines of the fires, including the Canadian Armed Forces, which assisted with the evacuation of members of Eabametoong First Nation , as well as host communities such as Thunder Bay.

Feds announce $4.7B for new Via Rail cars to be built in Ontario, Quebec

“More can be done in terms of investing in firefighting and aircraft and other equipment. More can be done working with communities, particularly Indigenous communities on both traditional methods [of] countering fires, but also for preparations for evacuations and others as those become necessary,” the prime minister said.

After Carney’s announcement at Alstom train manufacturer, he visited the Thunder Bay Fire Management Centre to meet wildland firefighters and hear about their efforts this season.

Outside the fire management centre, Carney was met with a lone member of Citizens United for a Sustainable Planet, a local environmental advocacy group.

Paul Berger, the group’s lead organizer, stood with a sign that read “Carbon Carney: Our Prime Arsonist.”

Paul Berger is lead organizer with Citizens United for a Sustainable Planet, an environmental advocacy group in Thunder Bay, Ont. He stood outside the Thunder Bay Fire Management Centre on Thursday ahead of Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit there, holding a sign that said “Carbon Carney: Our Prime Arsonist.” (Sarah Law/CBC) While Berger welcomed Carney’s investment in passenger rail services, he said the government should not be spending money on projects to promote fossil fuels, referring to the Canada-Alberta deal to build a new oil pipeline to the West Coast.

“To build rail cars and try to get people moving in trains while you're building pipelines is like being in a leaky boat and drilling holes in the hull and then getting a Dixie cup to bail. It's not adequate,” Berger said.

“We need much, much tougher climate policies, and we can have climate policies that also make life more affordable and better for Canadians.”

Thunder Bay, Ont., is seen covered in a thick blanket of smoke due to forest fires on July 14, 2026. (Marc Doucette/CBC) The federal government released a summary of findings from the second edition of Canada's Changing Climate Report on Thursday, which says Canada is projected to warm through this century with an estimated temperature increase of 5 C by 2081 to 2100.

“I think we have to help Canadians understand that climate isn't something that's just nice to have. It's absolutely imperative and the future generations are not going to forgive us for focusing on a war of words with the states,” Berger said, referencing the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade war.

“We need to do what we need to do for climate as well as everything else, and we could do those things together. We're just choosing not to do it.”

Nishnawbe Aski Nation Grand Chief Alvin Fiddler attends a news conference in Thunder Bay, Ont. on July 21, 2026. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press) Nishnawbe Aski Nation (NAN), a political-territorial organization that represents 49 First Nations in treaties 9 and 5, posted a statement about climate change and critical infrastructure on Thursday following Carney’s visit to Thunder Bay.

“More than 30 First Nation communities in northern Ontario have no year-round road access, relying on winter roads that are increasingly threatened by climate change. As temperatures rise, the season for these roads grows shorter every year, cutting communities off from essential goods, services and emergency response they depend on,” the statement said.

Canadians should prepare for a 5 C hotter future, report warns

“The prime minister talked today about investing in infrastructure that will secure ‘our future.’ We see nothing in his announcement so far to convince us that First Nations are included in that future,” NAN Grand Chief Alvin Fiddler continued in Thursday’s news release.

“We are calling on Canada to prove otherwise with the same ambition, the same urgency, and the same scale of investment.”

Sarah Law is a CBC News reporter based in Thunder Bay, Ont., and has also worked for newspapers and online publications elsewhere in the province. Have a story tip? You can reach her at sarah.law@cbc.ca.

title: Toronto police announce arrest in arson that damaged MP’s vehicle
sourceDescription: Threatening behaviour toward politicians in general has been on the rise in recent years
sourceBodyText:
Find clarity in the chaos. Subscribe now and save 70% SUBSCRIBE FROM $0.99/WEEK Digital access Digital + home delivery Toronto police announce arrest in arson that damaged MP’s vehicle Matthew Frank Published 4 hours ago Open this photo in gallery: MP Salma Zahid poses for a photograph beside her car which was set on fire overnight in the driveway of her home in Scarborough, in Toronto on August 27, 2026. Arlyn McAdorey/The Globe and Mail

Toronto police have arrested and charged one suspect and are searching for another for allegedly setting multiple cars on fire outside an east Toronto MP’s home.

In the early morning on Aug. 27, a suspect allegedly poured gas on vehicles parked outside the home of Liberal MP Salma Zahid in the Scarborough area of Toronto and set two on fire, damaging a third car, police said in a Friday news release.

The level of threats and abuse faced by MPs across all parties has spiked in recent years.

Police and firefighters responded to a 1:21 a.m. call about the fires, they said. No injuries were reported.

Roshvin Crofton, 24, was arrested on Aug. 30 and faces five charges, including arson causing to property and mischief over $5,000, Toronto police said in a news release. Investigators are still searching for another suspect in the alleged arson and are looking for any information involving a black 2025 Hyundai Sonata between Aug. 23 and Aug. 27, police said.

Ms. Zahid said in a statement that she welcomes both the arrest and news that police are seeking another person connected to the case. The investigation is ongoing and there’s no information on a motive, she said.

“With the support of my colleagues and with the guidance of security professionals, I will continue my work representing the people of Scarborough Centre-Don Valley East and I look forward to returning to Ottawa when the House of Commons resumes sitting later this month,” she said.

Ms. Zahid, who represents the riding of Scarborough Centre-Don Valley East, was first elected in 2015.

It’s the second time in nearly two years that a vehicle was allegedly set ablaze in front of a home on Ms. Zahid’s street. The 2024 case, which occurred outside an address a few houses away from the MP’s, is still being investigated, police said.

Both Prime Minister Mark Carney and federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre previously condemned the alleged arson in August.

Sergeant-at-Arms Patrick McDonell previously told a House of Commons standing committee that the number of security files his office opened on threatening behaviour towards MPs climbed from eight in 2019 to 530 in 2023. Threats and harassment against federal politicians also increased by 700 per cent in the same time frame, he said in 2024.

Female MPs in particular have been targeted with abuse and death threats .

In 2022, a man approached and aggressively harassed former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland in rural Alberta, and called her a traitor who should leave the province.

Liberal MP Iqra Khalid, who represents Mississauga-Erin Mills, said in 2024 that people have spat at her and made threats against her life. Members of a right-wing extremist organization had stalked her office and shared her address, she said, as well as videotaped her as she walked around her community.

Former environment minister Catherine McKenna spoke out when she was in office about the threats and harassment she received, which led her to request additional security.

RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme has suggested the federal government draft new laws that make it easier to charge people who threaten elected officials.

Internal RCMP documents from 2024 warned protecting parliamentarians and other public figures put a “significant strain” on personnel.
